lesson_title: Those Circles on the Farm Are Not From Aliens
hook_text: Fly over South African farmland and you will see giant perfect circles. On your orthophoto, they are worth marks.
clip_script: This is an orthophoto, an aerial photograph straightened by a computer so that it has the same scale everywhere. One centimetre is 100 metres. No symbols, no key. So how do you know what anything is? Seven questions. Dark or light? Smooth or rough? Shape? Size? Pattern? Shadow? What is next to it? Now look at the farmland. Perfect circles, some dark green, some pale. People build neat shapes; nature does not. These are centre-pivot irrigation: a sprinkler arm hundreds of metres long, turning around a point in the middle. Green circles are growing crops. Pale ones are bare soil. Next to the railway, long rectangles with big flat roofs: factories. Neat rows of small roofs: a planned suburb. Tiny roofs squeezed together with winding paths: an informal settlement. And the shadows all point the same way: south, because in South Africa the midday sun is in the north.
visual_style: An aerial view zooms down onto farmland with green and pale circles; a sprinkler arm sweeps around one; labels pop onto factories, suburbs and an informal settlement; a pylon's shadow stretches south with a compass arrow.
pacing: Mysterious hook, quick seven questions, a held moment on the circles, rapid town tour, crisp shadow ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for vertical and oblique photos, how orthophotos are made and reading land use with evidence.
